title: List the five patterns of cellular adaptation.
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: List the five patterns of cellular adaptation.
body.back: Hypertrophy (↑ cell size), hyperplasia (↑ cell number), atrophy (↓ cell size/number), metaplasia (change of mature cell type), dysplasia (disordered growth).

title: Hypertrophy vs hyperplasia — what changes in each?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Hypertrophy vs hyperplasia — what changes in each?
body.back: Hypertrophy: cell SIZE increases, cell number unchanged (non-dividing cells: heart, nerve, skeletal muscle). Hyperplasia: cell NUMBER increases (only possible in cells that can still divide).

title: Define atrophy and give two physiological and two pathological causes.
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Define atrophy and give two physiological and two pathological causes.
body.back: Shrinkage in cell size/number from decreased activity, usually reversible. Physiological: ageing, menopause/hormonal decline, thymic involution. Pathological: malnutrition, denervation, chronic ischaemia, pressure, disuse, coeliac disease.

title: Hypoplasia vs aplasia?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Hypoplasia vs aplasia?
body.back: Hypoplasia: congenital underdevelopment of an organ/tissue that did form. Aplasia (agenesis): the organ is wholly or largely absent due to a developmental defect.

title: Define metaplasia and give the classic oesophageal example.
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Define metaplasia and give the classic oesophageal example.
body.back: Reversible replacement of one mature differentiated cell type by another better suited to the stress. Example: Barrett's oesophagus — squamous mucosa replaced by columnar/intestinal-type epithelium from chronic acid/bile reflux.

title: What drives metaplasia at the molecular level?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What drives metaplasia at the molecular level?
body.back: Cytokines, growth factors and extracellular matrix signals reprogram tissue stem cells toward a different, fully differentiated cell lineage; it reverses once the stimulus stops.

title: Define dysplasia and its clinical significance.
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Define dysplasia and its clinical significance.
body.back: Disordered cellular growth: loss of uniformity in cell size/shape and loss of normal architectural polarity. It is precancerous and can progress toward carcinoma in situ / invasive cancer.

title: What is the progression sequence seen in Barrett's oesophagus?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is the progression sequence seen in Barrett's oesophagus?
body.back: Chronic reflux → squamous-to-columnar (intestinal) metaplasia → dysplasia → adenocarcinoma.

title: What causes benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) and how is it treated medically?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What causes benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) and how is it treated medically?
body.back: Androgen (DHT)-driven stromal growth of the prostate, causing urinary retention/nocturia. Treated with alpha-blockers (e.g. tamsulosin) or 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors (e.g. finasteride).

title: Name four growth factors that drive hyperplasia and one hormone example.
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Name four growth factors that drive hyperplasia and one hormone example.
body.back: EGF, PDGF, TGF-β, VEGF; hormonal example: oestrogen driving endometrial hyperplasia (androgens/DHT driving BPH; TSH driving thyroid hyperplasia).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Adaptation. Reversible change in size, number, phenotype or metabolism.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Atrophy. Smaller cells and fewer cells: ageing, disuse, denervation, ischaemia.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Cell death. Necrosis or apoptosis when injury becomes irreversible.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Dysplasia. Disordered growth with atypia; precancerous.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Normal cell in homeostasis. The steady state; stress pushes the cell to adapt or to be injured.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Hyperplasia. More cells: endometrium, liver regeneration, BPH, goitre.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Hypertrophy. Bigger cells, same number: heart, skeletal muscle, pregnant uterus.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Cell injury. Reversible if mild and transient, irreversible if severe and progressive.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Metaplasia. One mature cell type replaced by another: Barrett's, smoker's bronchus.

title: Physiological vs pathological adaptation?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Physiological vs pathological adaptation?
body.back: Physiological: response to normal stimulation (hormones, mediators), e.g. breast growth. Pathological: the way cells escape injury under abnormal stress.

title: Mechanisms of atrophy at the cellular level?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Mechanisms of atrophy at the cellular level?
body.back: Less protein production (low nutrients, hormones, energy) and more breakdown (proteasomes, lysosomes, inflammation).

title: Epithelial metaplasia types and risks?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Epithelial metaplasia types and risks?
body.back: Squamous (bronchus in smokers, bladder in schistosomiasis/stones → squamous cell carcinoma); columnar/intestinal (Barrett's, H. pylori stomach → adenocarcinoma).

title: Barrett's oesophagus histology?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Barrett's oesophagus histology?
body.back: Columnar metaplasia replacing squamous cells, intestinal-type glands with goblet cells, variable dysplasia; macroscopically pink mucosa, long (>30 mm) or short.

title: Three physiological causes of atrophy with numbers?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Three physiological causes of atrophy with numbers?
body.back: Ageing (30–40% muscle loss after 70, 5% brain volume per decade after 40, lipofuscin), hormonal decline at menopause/andropause, thymic involution (95% reduction).

title: Six pathological causes of atrophy?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Six pathological causes of atrophy?
body.back: Malnutrition/marasmus, denervation, chronic ischaemia, pressure (tumour, amyloid), disuse/immobilisation, autoimmune (coeliac villous atrophy).

title: Pure vs mixed hypertrophy?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Pure vs mixed hypertrophy?
body.back: Pure: only cell enlargement, in terminally differentiated cells (cardiac, nerve, skeletal muscle). Mixed: hypertrophy plus hyperplasia in cells that can divide (epithelium, smooth muscle, e.g. gravid uterus).

title: Why does cardiac hypertrophy eventually fail?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Why does cardiac hypertrophy eventually fail?
body.back: Function rises to a plateau; beyond it the thickened muscle weakens, leading to heart failure — a pathological adaptation to hypertension or aortic stenosis.

title: Growth factors and hormones in hyperplasia?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Growth factors and hormones in hyperplasia?
body.back: EGF (epithelium), PDGF (wound healing), TGF-β (fibroblasts), VEGF (vessels); oestrogen (endometrium), DHT (prostate), thyroid hormones (Graves), prolactin (breast).

title: Physiological hyperplasia examples?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Physiological hyperplasia examples?
body.back: Hormonal: breast and endometrium in pregnancy/cycle. Compensatory: liver after partial hepatectomy (mitoses from 12 h), marrow after blood loss, bone growth in childhood.

title: Pathological hyperplasia examples?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Pathological hyperplasia examples?
body.back: Chronic irritation: skin callus. Excess hormones: BPH (DHT), nodular thyroid hyperplasia/multinodular goitre, endometrial hyperplasia (cancer precursor).

title: Causes of metaplasia?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Causes of metaplasia?
body.back: Chronic irritation (reflux, smoke, alcohol), infections (H. pylori, HPV), physical stress (bile reflux, radiation), hormones (apocrine metaplasia), vitamin A deficiency, autoimmune gastritis.

title: Define carcinogenesis.
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Define carcinogenesis.
body.back: Non-lethal genetic damage (acquired from chemicals, radiation, viruses, or inherited) leading to clonal expansion of a single progenitor cell with growth and survival advantages; a multistep process (initiation → promotion → progression).

title: Four classes of genes targeted in carcinogenesis?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Four classes of genes targeted in carcinogenesis?
body.back: Proto-oncogenes (growth-promoting), tumour suppressor genes (growth-inhibiting), apoptosis regulators, DNA-repair genes.

title: Four stages of cancer evolution and three routes of metastasis?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Four stages of cancer evolution and three routes of metastasis?
body.back: Local (dysplasia/in situ) → locoregional (invasive) → generalisation (emboli) → metastasis. Routes: lymphatic (carcinomas), haematogenous (sarcomas, renal cell, follicular thyroid), transcoelomic (ovarian to peritoneum).

title: Oncogenes vs tumour suppressor genes?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Oncogenes vs tumour suppressor genes?
body.back: Oncogenes: mutated/overexpressed proto-oncogenes, gain of function, dominant (KRAS, EGFR). Suppressors: loss of function needed; governors (RB) brake proliferation, guardians (TP53) control genomic damage.

title: Classify chemical carcinogens.
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Classify chemical carcinogens.
body.back: Initiators: direct-acting (alkylating agents, anticancer drugs, acylating agents) or indirect-acting needing P-450 activation (benzopyrene, β-naphthylamine, benzidine, azo dyes). Promoters: not carcinogenic alone but stimulate proliferation of initiated cells.

title: Oncogenic viruses and their cancers?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Oncogenic viruses and their cancers?
body.back: HPV 16/18 (E6→p53, E7→RB): cervical/anogenital/oropharyngeal SCC. EBV (LMP1): Burkitt lymphoma. HHV8: Kaposi sarcoma. HBV: hepatocellular carcinoma. HTLV-1 (TAX): T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma.

title: Key translocations to know?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Key translocations to know?
body.back: t(8;14) MYC – Burkitt lymphoma; t(14;18) BCL2 – follicular lymphoma; t(9;22) BCR-ABL (Philadelphia) – CML; t(11;22) EWS-FLI1 – Ewing sarcoma.

title: Four ways genes are altered in cancer, with an example each?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Four ways genes are altered in cancer, with an example each?
body.back: Base substitution (BRAF V600E, EGFR L858R); indels (EGFR exon 19 del, RB 13q14 del, 17p del/p53); copy-number (HER2, NMYC amplification; CDKN2A loss); rearrangements/fusions (ALK, RET, NTRK, BCR-ABL).

title: List the seven hallmarks of cancer.
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: List the seven hallmarks of cancer.
body.back: Self-sufficiency in growth signals; insensitivity to growth inhibitors; evasion of cell death; limitless replicative potential; sustained angiogenesis; invasion and metastasis; immune evasion.

title: Four steps of ECM invasion?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Four steps of ECM invasion?
body.back: 1. Loosening of cells (E-cadherin loss). 2. Proteolytic degradation of basement membrane/ECM (MMPs, cathepsin D, urokinase). 3. Altered attachment to ECM (integrins). 4. Migration through the matrix to reach vessels.

title: Antitumour immune mechanisms?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Antitumour immune mechanisms?
body.back: CD8+ CTLs (dominant, MHC I-restricted), NK cells (first line, no sensitisation), M1 macrophages (IFN-γ, ROS, TNF), humoral/monoclonal antibodies (rituximab anti-CD20).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Carcinogenic agents. Chemicals, radiation and microbes acting in concert or sequence.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Clonal expansion. Tumours are monoclonal: one damaged progenitor with a growth advantage.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Dissemination. Lymphatic (carcinomas), haematogenous (sarcomas), transcoelomic (ovary).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Target genes. Proto-oncogenes, tumour suppressors, apoptosis regulators, DNA-repair genes.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Hallmarks of cancer. Self-sufficiency, insensitivity, evasion of death, immortality, angiogenesis, invasion, immune evasion.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Initiation and promotion. Initiators damage DNA; promoters make initiated cells proliferate.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Invasion of the matrix. Loosening (E-cadherin), proteolysis (MMPs), altered attachment, migration.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Metastasis. Micrometastases grow into macroscopic secondary tumours.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Tumour progression. Independent mutations create subclones with greater malignant potential.

title: Cell-cycle phases and checkpoints?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Cell-cycle phases and checkpoints?
body.back: G1 growth, S DNA replication, G2 preparation, M mitosis. Checkpoints: G1/S (DNA integrity, nutrients), G2/M (complete replication), metaphase/anaphase (chromosome attachment).

title: Normal vs cancer cell in the cycle?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Normal vs cancer cell in the cycle?
body.back: Normal: tight checkpoints, limited proliferation, arrest/repair on damage, apoptosis when needed. Cancer: dysregulated, uncontrolled, ignores stop signals, apoptosis often disabled.

title: How do tumours become immortal and vascularised?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: How do tumours become immortal and vascularised?
body.back: Reactivating telomerase; hypoxia → HIF-1α → VEGF driving neoangiogenesis and vasculogenesis (leaky, disorganised vessels); anti-VEGF bevacizumab.

title: Classes of tumour antigens?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Classes of tumour antigens?
body.back: Mutated oncogene/suppressor products (RAS, BCR-ABL, p53), overexpressed (tyrosinase, gp100, MART), cancer-testis (MAGE, BAGE), viral (HPV E6/E7), oncofetal (CEA, AFP), differentiation antigens.

title: Precursor lesions: sure vs possible?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Precursor lesions: sure vs possible?
body.back: Sure (genetic): familial adenomatous polyposis, xeroderma pigmentosum. Possible (acquired): colonic adenoma, ulcerative colitis, bladder papilloma, gastric atrophy, cirrhosis.

title: Direct-acting chemical carcinogens?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Direct-acting chemical carcinogens?
body.back: Alkylating agents (β-propiolactone, dimethyl sulfate), anticancer drugs (cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil, nitrosoureas), acylating agents.

title: Indirect-acting chemical carcinogens?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Indirect-acting chemical carcinogens?
body.back: Need cytochrome P-450 activation: polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (benzopyrene, benzanthracene), aromatic amines/azo dyes (β-naphthylamine, benzidine, butter yellow).

title: How does H. pylori cause cancer?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: How does H. pylori cause cancer?
body.back: Immune-mediated chronic inflammation, stimulation of gastric proliferation, reactive oxygen species damaging DNA, growth-factor pathways via CagA → adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma.

title: Governors vs guardians among tumour suppressors?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Governors vs guardians among tumour suppressors?
body.back: Governors brake proliferation (RB; loss removes the brake). Guardians control genomic damage (TP53; loss allows mutation accumulation).

title: Copy-number alterations to know?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Copy-number alterations to know?
body.back: Amplifications of oncogenes: HER2 (breast, 20%), NMYC (neuroblastoma, 25–30%). Deletions of suppressors: CDKN2A (p16/p14).

title: How do translocations activate proto-oncogenes?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: How do translocations activate proto-oncogenes?
body.back: By placing them under an active promoter (MYC in Burkitt t(8;14), BCL2 in follicular lymphoma t(14;18)) or by creating fusion proteins (BCR-ABL in CML, EWS-FLI1 in Ewing).

title: The colorectal multistep model?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: The colorectal multistep model?
body.back: Normal → hyperproliferative epithelium (APC 5q) → early adenoma (hypomethylation) → intermediate adenoma (RAS 12p) → late adenoma (18q loss) → carcinoma (p53 17p).

title: Self-sufficiency in growth signals: mechanisms?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Self-sufficiency in growth signals: mechanisms?
body.back: Autocrine loops (PDGF in glioblastoma), stromal growth factors, overexpressed/mutant receptors (HER2), self-activated downstream signalling, deregulated transcription factors.

title: Define necrosis.
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Define necrosis.
body.back: Cell death with severe membrane damage: lysosomal enzymes digest the cell, contents leak out and elicit inflammation. Always pathological and irreversible.

title: Define apoptosis.
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Define apoptosis.
body.back: Programmed cell death: the cell activates caspases that degrade its own DNA and proteins, fragments into membrane-bound apoptotic bodies that are phagocytosed without inflammation.

title: Three nuclear changes of necrosis, in order?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Three nuclear changes of necrosis, in order?
body.back: Pyknosis (shrinkage/condensation) → karyorrhexis (fragmentation) → karyolysis (dissolution). The nucleus disappears in 1–2 days.

title: Six patterns of tissue necrosis and one example each.
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Six patterns of tissue necrosis and one example each.
body.back: Coagulative (infarct, except brain); liquefactive (abscess, brain infarct); caseous (TB); gangrenous (ischaemic limb); fat necrosis (pancreatitis, breast trauma); fibrinoid (polyarteritis nodosa).

title: Necrosis vs apoptosis: cell size, membrane, inflammation, role?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Necrosis vs apoptosis: cell size, membrane, inflammation, role?
body.back: Necrosis: enlarged, disrupted membrane, inflammation yes, always pathological. Apoptosis: reduced, intact membrane, no inflammation, often physiological.

title: Give four physiological causes of apoptosis.
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Give four physiological causes of apoptosis.
body.back: Embryogenesis; involution of hormone-dependent tissues (menstrual endometrium, breast after weaning); turnover of intestinal crypt cells; removal of neutrophils/lymphocytes after inflammation or immune response; CTL killing of infected or tumour cells.

title: Give three pathological causes of apoptosis.
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Give three pathological causes of apoptosis.
body.back: DNA damage (radiation, cytotoxic drugs); accumulation of misfolded proteins; some viral infections (adenovirus, HIV).

title: Which caspases are activators and which are executioners?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Which caspases are activators and which are executioners?
body.back: Activators: 2, 8, 9, 10. Executioners: 3, 6, 7 (DNA fragmentation, chromatin condensation, membrane changes).

title: Intrinsic vs extrinsic apoptosis pathway?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Intrinsic vs extrinsic apoptosis pathway?
body.back: Intrinsic (mitochondrial, most frequent): internal triggers, BCL-2 vs Bax/Bak balance, caspase 9. Extrinsic (death receptor): external signal, Fas/FasL, caspase 8.

title: How do BCL-2 and p53 relate to cancer?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: How do BCL-2 and p53 relate to cancer?
body.back: BCL-2 overexpression (follicular lymphoma) blocks apoptosis. p53 guards the G1/S checkpoint and triggers Bax-mediated apoptosis when DNA damage is irreparable; p53 mutations are common in cancers. Therapies: anti-BCL2 drugs, chemo/radiotherapy.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Apoptosis. Programmed suicide; the membrane stays intact.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Executioner caspases. 3, 6 and 7 fragment DNA and reshape the cell.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Extrinsic (death receptor) pathway. Outside signal such as FasL on activated T cells; caspase 8.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Inflammation. Leaked contents attract leukocytes; only after necrosis.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Irreversible injury. Severe or progressive stress beyond repair.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway. The most frequent; balance of BCL-2 versus Bax/Bak; converges on caspase 9.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Necrosis. Enzymes leak, cell bursts, contents spill out.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Clearance of apoptotic bodies. Macrophages remove fragments before anything leaks.

title: What determines the cell's response to aggression?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What determines the cell's response to aggression?
body.back: The cause, severity and duration of the aggression, and the type and adaptive capacity of the cell.

title: Why does necrosis cause inflammation but apoptosis does not?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Why does necrosis cause inflammation but apoptosis does not?
body.back: Necrosis ruptures the membrane and spills contents that elicit a host reaction; apoptotic bodies keep an intact membrane and are cleared before leaking.

title: Cytoplasmic changes of necrosis?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Cytoplasmic changes of necrosis?
body.back: Increased eosinophilia (denatured proteins bind eosin, RNA loss removes basophilia) and a homogeneous glassy look from glycogen loss.

title: Causes of necrosis?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Causes of necrosis?
body.back: Anoxia/ischaemia, physical agents, chemicals and drugs, infections, immune reactions, nutritional imbalance.

title: Coagulative vs liquefactive necrosis?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Coagulative vs liquefactive necrosis?
body.back: Coagulative: architecture preserved, anucleate ghosts, infarcts except brain. Liquefactive: complete enzymatic digestion into liquid, infections and brain infarcts.

title: Where is fat necrosis seen?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Where is fat necrosis seen?
body.back: Acute pancreatitis (activated lipases in the peritoneum, an emergency) and breast trauma (cytosteatonecrosis).

title: Physiological roles of apoptosis in immunity?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Physiological roles of apoptosis in immunity?
body.back: Removing neutrophils after acute inflammation, lymphocytes after an immune response, and killing infected/neoplastic cells via cytotoxic T lymphocytes.

title: How do BCL-2 and Bax/Bak interact?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: How do BCL-2 and Bax/Bak interact?
body.back: BCL-2 is anti-apoptotic and prevents Bax/Bak from permeabilising mitochondria; p53 activates Bax when DNA damage is irreparable.

title: What does Fas ligand do?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What does Fas ligand do?
body.back: Membrane protein on activated T lymphocytes that engages Fas death receptors on target cells, activating caspase 8 (extrinsic pathway).

title: Recap: how does necrosis compare with apoptosis in frequency and extent?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Recap: how does necrosis compare with apoptosis in frequency and extent?
body.back: Necrosis is less frequent, involves many cells, may not be localised, is uncontrolled and pathological, with inflammation; apoptosis is often single cells, controlled, no inflammation.

title: What is the sequence from homeostasis to cell death?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is the sequence from homeostasis to cell death?
body.back: Homeostasis → stress → adaptation; if unable to adapt → reversible injury (repair) or, if severe, irreversible injury → cell death (necrosis or apoptosis).

title: List the major acquired causes of cell injury.
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: List the major acquired causes of cell injury.
body.back: Physical agents, chemicals and drugs, microbial agents, immunologic agents, ageing (plus genetic causes as the other major group).

title: Describe the ischaemic pathway of cell injury.
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Describe the ischaemic pathway of cell injury.
body.back: No blood flow → no oxygen → mitochondria cannot make ATP → membrane pumps fail → calcium accumulates → poisons mitochondria, damages proteins/DNA, activates enzymes that damage membranes.

title: What does the outcome of cell injury depend on?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What does the outcome of cell injury depend on?
body.back: Type, duration and severity of the agent; type, status and adaptability of the target cell; intracellular events (mitochondrial damage, free radicals); morphological consequences.

title: Signs of reversible cell injury under the microscope?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Signs of reversible cell injury under the microscope?
body.back: Membrane blebs, swollen endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria, myelin figures (phospholipids from damaged membranes).

title: Name the four morphological forms of reversible injury (degenerations).
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Name the four morphological forms of reversible injury (degenerations).
body.back: Hydropic change, hyaline change, mucoid change, fatty change.

title: Give examples of intracellular and extracellular hyaline change.
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Give examples of intracellular and extracellular hyaline change.
body.back: Intracellular: hyaline droplets (proteinuria), Zenker's degeneration (typhoid), Mallory bodies (alcohol), Russell bodies (plasma cells). Extracellular: leiomyoma, old scars, hyaline arteriolosclerosis (hypertension, diabetes).

title: How do epithelial mucin and connective-tissue mucin stain?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: How do epithelial mucin and connective-tissue mucin stain?
body.back: Both: Alcian blue positive. Epithelial mucin: PAS positive. Connective-tissue (myxoid) mucin: PAS negative, colloidal iron positive.

title: Necrosis vs apoptosis in one line each?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Necrosis vs apoptosis in one line each?
body.back: Necrosis: the cell bursts, releases contents and attracts inflammatory cells. Apoptosis: quiet, programmed death encoded in the cell's DNA.

title: Why does cardiac muscle fare worse than skeletal muscle in hypoxia?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Why does cardiac muscle fare worse than skeletal muscle in hypoxia?
body.back: Cardiac muscle is highly susceptible and is irreversibly injured after more than 20 minutes; skeletal muscle can withstand hypoxia for a long time.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: ATP depletion. Without oxygen mitochondria cannot make ATP; injury starts here.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Calcium overload. Calcium accumulates in the cytoplasm.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Calcium damage. Poisons mitochondria, damages proteins and DNA, activates enzymes that destroy membranes.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Irreversible injury. Nuclear hallmarks, then necrosis or apoptosis.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Ischaemia / hypoxia. The most common cause of cell injury.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Membrane damage. Free radicals attack the cell membrane.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Membrane pump failure. Without ATP the ion pumps stop working.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Free radicals. The second major cause: from inflammation, radiation, chemicals and toxins.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Reversible injury. Membrane blebs, swollen ER and mitochondria, myelin figures.

title: Main organelles and their roles?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Main organelles and their roles?
body.back: Plasma membrane (exchange), mitochondria (ATP), rough ER (proteins), smooth ER (lipids, detox), Golgi (packaging), lysosomes (digestion), peroxisomes (detox), cytoskeleton (shape/transport), centrioles (division).

title: Physical agents that injure cells?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Physical agents that injure cells?
body.back: Mechanical trauma, thermal injury (heat, cold), electricity, UV and ionising radiation, rapid change in atmospheric pressure.

title: Chemical agents that injure cells?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Chemical agents that injure cells?
body.back: Cyanide, arsenic, mercury, strong acids/alkalis, pollutants, pesticides, high-concentration oxygen, hypertonic glucose/salt, alcohol, narcotics, therapeutic drugs.

title: Why does hypoxia harm the heart faster than skeletal muscle?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Why does hypoxia harm the heart faster than skeletal muscle?
body.back: Susceptibility depends on the target cell: cardiac muscle is irreversibly injured after more than 20 minutes; skeletal muscle withstands hypoxia much longer.

title: Two basic causes of cell injury per the lecture's simple model?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Two basic causes of cell injury per the lecture's simple model?
body.back: 1. Ischaemia (no oxygen → no ATP → pump failure → calcium). 2. Free radicals (inflammation, radiation, chemicals, toxins → membrane damage).

title: Morphology of hydropic change in the kidney?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Morphology of hydropic change in the kidney?
body.back: Swollen tubular epithelial cells with small clear cytoplasmic vacuoles and blebs; grossly the kidney is enlarged with a bulging cut surface.

title: Define hyaline.
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Define hyaline.
body.back: 'Glassy': a homogeneous, eosinophilic proteinaceous appearance on H&E; a descriptive term, not a specific substance; intracellular or extracellular.

title: Where does mucin come from, and how does it stain?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Where does mucin come from, and how does it stain?
body.back: Epithelial cells of mucous membranes/glands (epithelial mucin, PAS+) and connective-tissue cells (myxoid, PAS−, colloidal iron+); both Alcian blue+.

title: Define fatty change.
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Define fatty change.
body.back: Intracellular accumulation of neutral fat in parenchymal cells, especially the liver; also heart, skeletal muscle, kidney (lipoid nephrosis).

title: Processes of cell death listed in the lecture?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Processes of cell death listed in the lecture?
body.back: Locally: autolysis, necrosis, apoptosis. Following local death: gangrene, calcification.

title: Define inflammation and its two goals.
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Define inflammation and its two goals.
body.back: The response of living vascularised tissue to injury, in the vascular connective tissue; it aims to eliminate/isolate the aggressor and repair the tissue.

title: Cardinal signs of acute inflammation and their laboratory correlates?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Cardinal signs of acute inflammation and their laboratory correlates?
body.back: Rubor, tumor, calor, dolor (Celsus) + loss of function (Virchow). Biology: leukocytosis, raised ESR and CRP.

title: Acute vs chronic inflammation in one line each?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Acute vs chronic inflammation in one line each?
body.back: Acute: immediate, vasculo-exudative, neutrophils, days to weeks, usually heals. Chronic: persistent agent, mononuclear cells + fibrosis, months to years, no spontaneous recovery.

title: List plasma-derived and cell-derived mediators.
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: List plasma-derived and cell-derived mediators.
body.back: Plasma: complement, kinins (bradykinin), coagulation/fibrinolysis (factor XII). Cellular: histamine, serotonin, PAF, nitric oxide, arachidonic-acid metabolites, cytokines (IL-1, TNF-α, IL-6 pro; IL-4, IL-10, IL-13 anti).

title: What are the three stages of the vascular reaction?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What are the three stages of the vascular reaction?
body.back: Congestion (vasodilatation → redness, heat), inflammatory oedema (permeability → exudate, swelling, pain), leukocyte diapedesis (margination, rolling, adhesion, transmigration, chemotaxis).

title: Roles of inflammatory oedema?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Roles of inflammatory oedema?
body.back: Dilutes toxins; delivers immunoglobulins and complement (opsonins) and fibrinogen (fibrin barrier); slows flow to promote diapedesis. Harmful if massive, sudden, or laryngeal/cerebral.

title: Three phases of phagocytosis?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Three phases of phagocytosis?
body.back: Recognition/adhesion (opsonins, Toll-like receptors) → ingestion (pseudopods → phagosome) → digestion (phagolysosome with acidic pH and hydrolytic enzymes).

title: Internal vs external debridement?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Internal vs external debridement?
body.back: Internal: macrophages phagocytose neutrophils; oedema drains via lymphatics/veins. External: spontaneous fistulisation or surgical incision. Incomplete debridement → chronicity.

title: Systemic effects of inflammation and their cytokines?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Systemic effects of inflammation and their cytokines?
body.back: Fever (TNF, IL-1 → hypothalamic prostaglandins); acute-phase proteins CRP, fibrinogen, SAA (IL-6 on liver); leukocytosis (CSFs); septic shock (high TNF).

title: Describe granulation tissue formation and its evolution.
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Describe granulation tissue formation and its evolution.
body.back: Appears 1–4 days: neo-vessels (angiogenesis via VEGF/angiopoietin), fibroblasts/myofibroblasts (TGF-β, PDGF, FGF, IGF), matrix with type III collagen. Remodels to type I collagen with retraction → fibrous scar, or restitution ad integrum.

title: Name the suppurative forms of inflammation.
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Name the suppurative forms of inflammation.
body.back: Pustule (in/under epidermis), abscess (localised cavity in a solid organ), phlegmon (diffuse, streptococcal hyaluronidase), empyema (pus in a natural cavity); necrotising inflammation adds necrosis (anaerobes, ischaemia).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Chemotaxis. Unidirectional migration along a gradient of bacterial products, complement or arachidonic-acid metabolites.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Chronic inflammation. If the agent persists: mononuclear cells and fibrosis, months to years.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Congestion. Arteriolar then capillary vasodilatation with slowed flow: redness and heat.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Leukocyte diapedesis. Neutrophils marginate, roll, adhere via selectins and cross the wall.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Inflammatory oedema. Endothelial gaps and permeability let a protein-rich exudate out: swelling and pain.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Inflammatory granuloma. The cells at the site: neutrophils in the first 6 to 24 h, then macrophages and lymphocytes.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Phagocytosis and debridement. Recognition, ingestion, digestion; cleansing of debris internally or externally.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Repair. Granulation tissue from 1 to 4 days, then scar or restitution ad integrum.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Initiation. Cellular aggression activates mast cells, which release histamine.

title: Which cells are 'other cells' of inflammation and what do they do?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Which cells are 'other cells' of inflammation and what do they do?
body.back: Fibroblasts/myofibroblasts (migration, proliferation, collagen and ECM synthesis, contraction) and endothelial cells (permeability, vasomotion, adhesion proteins, neovascularisation).

title: Origins and roles of macrophages?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Origins and roles of macrophages?
body.back: Marrow monoblast → blood monocyte → tissue histiocyte; initiate/modulate inflammation by cytokines, lyse bacteria with lysosomal proteinases, phagocytose.

title: Cutaneous repair abnormalities?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Cutaneous repair abnormalities?
body.back: Botriomycoma/pyogenic granuloma (exuberant bleeding granulation tissue) and keloid (collagen overproduction); also scars lacking adnexa and metaplastic regeneration.

title: Vascular complications of acute inflammation?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Vascular complications of acute inflammation?
body.back: Congestive (solar erythema), oedematous (exudative alveolitis), haemorrhagic (Waterhouse-Friderichsen adrenal haemorrhage), fibrinous (pericarditis).

title: Neutrophil enzymes?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Neutrophil enzymes?
body.back: Lysozyme, myeloperoxidase, phospholipase A2, hydrolases, interferons; plus chemotaxis and phagocytosis.

title: Mechanisms of increased vascular permeability?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Mechanisms of increased vascular permeability?
body.back: Endothelial contraction (gaps), endothelial necrosis/detachment (direct injury), fusion of intracellular vesicles (channels), leakage from immature new vessels.

title: Sources of chemotactic substances?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Sources of chemotactic substances?
body.back: Infectious agents, necrotic tissue, complement, arachidonic-acid metabolites; movement is unidirectional for neutrophils, macrophages and lymphocytes.

title: Exceptions to 'neutrophils first'?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Exceptions to 'neutrophils first'?
body.back: Viral infections: lymphocytes may arrive first. Some hypersensitivity reactions: eosinophils predominate.

title: Factors deciding the evolution of acute inflammation?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Factors deciding the evolution of acute inflammation?
body.back: Nature of the agent, severity of damage, host health and immune status, regenerative capacity of the tissue (labile, stable, permanent).

title: Mediators of resolution?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Mediators of resolution?
body.back: Short-lived mediators; acetylcholine inhibiting TNF-α; IL-1ra, IL-4, IL-10, IL-11, TGF-β; lipoxins; resolvins and protectins.

title: Stages of angiogenesis?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Stages of angiogenesis?
body.back: Basement-membrane degradation → endothelial migration → proliferation as solid buds → maturation into capillary tubes → recruitment of periendothelial cells.

title: Two possible ends of granulation tissue?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Two possible ends of granulation tissue?
body.back: Fibrous scarring (retraction and organisation of matrix replacing destroyed tissue) or restitution ad integrum (tissue identical to before).

title: Define pathology in one sentence.
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Define pathology in one sentence.
body.back: The branch of medicine studying the structural and functional changes in tissues and organs caused by disease, at macroscopic and microscopic level.

title: Aetiology vs pathogenesis — what's the difference?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Aetiology vs pathogenesis — what's the difference?
body.back: Aetiology = the CAUSE of disease (why it arises); pathogenesis = the MECHANISM by which that cause produces disease (how it develops).

title: What is a lesion, and what's the difference between an elementary lesion and a lesional complex?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is a lesion, and what's the difference between an elementary lesion and a lesional complex?
body.back: A lesion is any structural damage/abnormal change caused by disease. An elementary lesion affects one structure; a lesional complex is an association of several elementary lesions.

title: General pathology vs systematic pathology?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: General pathology vs systematic pathology?
body.back: General pathology studies basic disease mechanisms (cell injury, inflammation, circulatory disorders, neoplasia). Systematic pathology applies these mechanisms to specific organ systems.

title: Match the pioneer to their contribution: Morgagni, Virchow, Vesalius, Pasteur/Koch, Van Leeuwenhoek.
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Match the pioneer to their contribution: Morgagni, Virchow, Vesalius, Pasteur/Koch, Van Leeuwenhoek.
body.back: Morgagni: linked disease to organ changes (founded anatomic pathology). Virchow: father of cellular pathology. Vesalius: corrected Galenic anatomy (1543). Pasteur & Koch: germ theory of disease. Van Leeuwenhoek: invented the microscope.

title: What are the three levels at which lesions are examined?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What are the three levels at which lesions are examined?
body.back: Macroscopic (naked eye/magnifying glass), microscopic-tissue (pathological histology), microscopic-cellular (pathological cytology).

title: What does 'anatomo-clinical correlation' mean and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What does 'anatomo-clinical correlation' mean and why does it matter?
body.back: Correlating the pathologist's morphological findings with the patient's clinical data and paraclinical tests (imaging, biology) — essential for reaching a synthetic diagnosis.

title: Name the four roles of pathology in patient care.
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Name the four roles of pathology in patient care.
body.back: Diagnostic (establishing the diagnosis), prognostic (e.g. pTNM staging in cancer), evaluating response to therapy, and supporting research protocols.

title: Primary vs idiopathic aetiology?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Primary vs idiopathic aetiology?
body.back: Primary = the cause of disease is known. Idiopathic = the cause is unknown.

title: Human pathology vs experimental pathology?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Human pathology vs experimental pathology?
body.back: Human pathology examines structural abnormalities in patient tissue (gross and microscopic). Experimental pathology studies cellular processes using animal models and tissue/cell cultures.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Clinical manifestations. Symptoms and signs, course and prognosis determined by the lesions.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Anatomo-clinical diagnosis. Correlating the lesion with clinical, biological and imaging data.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Aetiology. The cause of disease: primary if known, idiopathic if unknown; genetic or acquired.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Morphological changes (lesion). Gross or microscopic structural alterations that follow the pathogenetic mechanism.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Pathogenesis. The mechanism by which the cause produces structural and functional abnormalities.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Prognosis and treatment. Pathology's roles: diagnosis, prognostic evaluation, response to therapy, research.

title: What does 'anatomical pathology' study, in the simplest terms?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What does 'anatomical pathology' study, in the simplest terms?
body.back: Any visible modification (lesion) in the body caused by disease — to the naked eye (macroscopy) or under the microscope (histology for tissues, cytology for cells).

title: Who were Morgagni, Virchow and Vesalius?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Who were Morgagni, Virchow and Vesalius?
body.back: Morgagni linked diseases to organ changes (founded anatomic pathology). Virchow: father of cellular pathology. Vesalius: corrected Galen's anatomy in 1543.

title: What are the four categories of lesions shown in the lecture?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What are the four categories of lesions shown in the lecture?
body.back: Malformative (e.g. arteriovenous malformation), inflammatory/immune (e.g. lung tuberculosis), circulatory (e.g. atherosclerosis), neoplastic (e.g. adenocarcinoma).

title: Why must the request form be complete?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Why must the request form be complete?
body.back: Because the clinical features, course and prognosis guide the pathologist's diagnostic process — the form is the pathologist's 'patient interview'.

title: What is the course of a disease?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is the course of a disease?
body.back: The stages of its natural history in the absence of intervention — for infections: incubation, prodrome, illness, decline, convalescence.

title: What did the clinical case teach?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What did the clinical case teach?
body.back: A lung nodule in a man with prior prostate cancer; IHC PSA+ and TTF-1− showed a solitary lung metastasis from prostate adenocarcinoma — pathology changes the diagnosis and the treatment.

title: Name four famous pathologists and their eponym.
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Name four famous pathologists and their eponym.
body.back: Papanicolaou (Pap smear), Langerhans (islets/cells), Hodgkin (Hodgkin disease), Reed (Reed-Sternberg cells), Spitz (Spitz naevus), Call-Exner bodies, Piringer-Kuchinka lymphadenitis.

title: How is pathology positioned among medical sciences?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: How is pathology positioned among medical sciences?
body.back: As the vital link between basic sciences (anatomy, physiology, biochemistry, pharmacology) and clinical sciences (medicine, surgery, neurology, dermatology).

title: Four future directions of pathology?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Four future directions of pathology?
body.back: Digital pathology for remote diagnosis, AI-driven predictions, single-cell sequencing, spatial transcriptomics.

title: What are the four aspects of a disease process pathology covers?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What are the four aspects of a disease process pathology covers?
body.back: Aetiology, pathogenesis, molecular and morphological changes, functional alterations/clinical manifestations.

title: Define a tumour (neoplasm).
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Define a tumour (neoplasm).
body.back: Excessive cellular proliferation forming a mass resembling the tissue of origin, persisting and growing, escaping normal controls of growth and differentiation; molecularly, a clonal disorder from acquired mutations in a single cell.

title: Four core characteristics of tumours?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Four core characteristics of tumours?
body.back: Excessive abnormal proliferation; biological autonomy (persists after stimulus); clonality (mono/oligo/polyclonal); differentiation (degree of resemblance to parent cell). Built by a multi-step accumulation of genetic errors.

title: Example of tumour progression as a continuum?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Example of tumour progression as a continuum?
body.back: Normal colorectal mucosa → adenoma with low-grade dysplasia → adenoma with high-grade dysplasia → colorectal carcinoma, by accumulation of molecular alterations.

title: Macroscopic differences benign vs malignant?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Macroscopic differences benign vs malignant?
body.back: Benign: well circumscribed, encapsulated, pushing borders, homogeneous cut surface. Malignant: poorly circumscribed, non-encapsulated, infiltrative/destructive, heterogeneous with necrosis and haemorrhage.

title: Microscopic differences benign vs malignant?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Microscopic differences benign vs malignant?
body.back: Benign: well differentiated, few normal mitoses, no cytonuclear abnormalities. Malignant: variably/undifferentiated, frequent abnormal mitoses, cytonuclear abnormalities (hyperchromatism, pleomorphism, multinucleation).

title: Dysplasia vs anaplasia?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Dysplasia vs anaplasia?
body.back: Dysplasia: intra-epithelial disordered growth with cellular atypia, graded mild/moderate/severe, then carcinoma in situ (no basement-membrane invasion). Anaplasia: complete undifferentiation, almost always malignant.

title: Grading vs staging?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Grading vs staging?
body.back: Grading: microscopic assessment of how abnormal the tumour looks (differentiation, pleomorphism, mitoses). Staging: how far it has spread — TNM (tumour, nodes, metastases) using imaging and pathology (pTNM).

title: Give the benign and malignant names for: glandular epithelium, squamous epithelium, fat, cartilage, bone, smooth muscle, striated muscle, vessels.
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Give the benign and malignant names for: glandular epithelium, squamous epithelium, fat, cartilage, bone, smooth muscle, striated muscle, vessels.
body.back: Adenoma/adenocarcinoma; papilloma/squamous cell carcinoma; lipoma/liposarcoma; chondroma/chondrosarcoma; osteoma/osteosarcoma; leiomyoma/leiomyosarcoma; rhabdomyoma/rhabdomyosarcoma; haemangioma/angiosarcoma.

title: Which '-oma' tumours are malignant?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Which '-oma' tumours are malignant?
body.back: Melanoma, lymphoma (and leukaemia), glioma.

title: What are pseudotumours? Give the three groups.
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What are pseudotumours? Give the three groups.
body.back: Lesions that do not meet criteria for a true neoplasm: inflammatory (chronic inflammation, foreign body, pyogenic granuloma, keloid), hormonal (goitre, gynaecomastia, adrenal/endometrial hyperplasia), developmental (heterotopia).

title: Teratomas and blastomas: key facts?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Teratomas and blastomas: key facts?
body.back: Teratomas: from pluripotent cells of the three germ layers; ovary/testis and midline sites; 95% mature-benign (ovary), 5% immature-malignant (testis). Blastomas: malignant childhood tumours from organ blastema (Wilms, retinoblastoma, medulloblastoma, hepatoblastoma); chondroblastoma and osteoblastoma are benign.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Benign tumour. Well circumscribed, encapsulated, well differentiated, no metastasis.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Dysplasia. Disordered growth with cellular atypia confined to the epithelium; mild, moderate, severe.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Grading. Microscopic score of differentiation, pleomorphism and mitoses.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Carcinoma in situ. Dysplastic cells fill the epithelium without crossing the basement membrane.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Invasive carcinoma. Infiltration and destruction of surrounding tissue.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Metastasis. Secondary implants at a distance; benign tumours cannot do this.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Normal tissue. Homeostatic proliferation, differentiation and apoptosis.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Pseudotumours. Inflammatory, hormonal or developmental lesions that mimic tumours.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Staging. TNM: tumour size, nodes, metastases, from imaging and pTNM.

title: Cancer epidemiology basics?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Cancer epidemiology basics?
body.back: 2nd cause of death after cardiovascular disease; commonest: prostate (men), breast (women); deadliest: lung in both; mortality declining with treatment advances.

title: Environmental causes of cancer?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Environmental causes of cancer?
body.back: Infections (HPV, HBV), smoking, alcohol, diet, obesity, oestrogen exposure/reproductive history, UV, arsenic, asbestos, benzene, radon.

title: Growth fraction and treatment?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Growth fraction and treatment?
body.back: GF = % of dividing cells. High GF (leukaemia, lymphoma, small-cell lung) → chemo/radiation. Low GF (breast, colon) → debulking.

title: Breast grading system?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Breast grading system?
body.back: Tubules (1–3), pleomorphism (1–3), mitoses per 10 hpf (0–9:1, 10–19:2, ≥20:3). Total 3–5 low (>95% 5-year survival), 6–7 intermediate (80%), 8–9 high (60%).

title: TNM categories?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: TNM categories?
body.back: T0 no tumour, Tis in situ, TX not assessable, T1–4 size; N0 no nodes, NX not assessable, N1–4 increasing nodes; M0 none, MX not assessable, M1–3 increasing metastases.

title: Inflammatory pseudotumours?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Inflammatory pseudotumours?
body.back: Chronic inflammation, foreign-body reaction, pyogenic granuloma, hypertrophic scar/keloid, pseudotumoral tuberculosis, schistosomal hepatic fibrosis, aspergilloma.

title: Benign tumour names by tissue?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Benign tumour names by tissue?
body.back: Fibroma, lipoma, chondroma, osteoma, rhabdomyoma, leiomyoma, haemangioma, lymphangioma; adenoma (glands), papilloma (squamous), cystadenoma, polyp.

title: Special tumour categories?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Special tumour categories?
body.back: Mixed tumours (adenosquamous carcinoma, carcinosarcoma, pleomorphic adenoma, fibroadenoma), teratomas, blastomas.

title: Prevention and early detection strategies?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Prevention and early detection strategies?
body.back: Avoid carcinogens (tobacco, alcohol); vaccination (HBV, HPV); screening at pre-invasive stages (Pap smear); pathogen detection (PCR); genetic screening (BRCA).

title: Possible evolutionary sequences of a lesion?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Possible evolutionary sequences of a lesion?
body.back: Benign may stay benign, become dysplasia, in situ, then invasive; dysplasia may go to in situ then invasive; in situ to invasive.

title: Hallmark properties acquired by tumour cells?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Hallmark properties acquired by tumour cells?
body.back: Own mitogenic signals, insensitivity to inhibition, evasion of death, immortality, invasion/metastasis, angiogenesis, aerobic glycolysis, immune evasion.

title: Evolution and prognosis: benign vs malignant?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Evolution and prognosis: benign vs malignant?
body.back: Benign: slow local growth, no relapse, good prognosis. Malignant: rapid growth, invasion, metastasis, relapse, poor prognosis if untreated.

title: Locally aggressive vs low-malignancy tumours?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Locally aggressive vs low-malignancy tumours?
body.back: Locally aggressive: benign morphology but invasive with relapse (desmoid tumour). Low malignancy: malignant morphology, locally aggressive (basal cell carcinoma).

title: Causes of dysplasia?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Causes of dysplasia?
body.back: Genetic mutations (oncogenes, suppressors, DNA repair), chronic inflammation, hormones (oestrogen), carcinogens (tobacco, UV, asbestos), infections (HPV, HBV/HCV).

title: Histological features of dysplasia?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Histological features of dysplasia?
body.back: Hypercellularity, cellular atypia (large hyperchromatic irregular nuclei, high N/C ratio), loss of polarity, increased and atypical mitoses, stromal changes.

title: Dysplasia by organ?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Dysplasia by organ?
body.back: Cervix: thickened epithelium, pleomorphism, atypical basal mitoses. Colon: nuclear enlargement, irregular crypts, superficial mitoses. Bronchus: basal hyperplasia, lost polarity. Skin: keratinocyte atypia, lost stratification.

title: Cytological vs histological specimen — what's the difference?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Cytological vs histological specimen — what's the difference?
body.back: Cytological: isolated cells only (FNA, Pap smear, fluids). Histological: cells plus tissue architecture (biopsy, surgical specimen, autopsy).

title: What are the main steps of histopathology processing, in order?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What are the main steps of histopathology processing, in order?
body.back: Fixation → dehydration (graded alcohols) → clearing → wax infiltration/impregnation → embedding (paraffin block) → section cutting (3–5 microns) → staining (H&E) → mounting → microscopy.

title: What does H&E staining show?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What does H&E staining show?
body.back: Haematoxylin stains nuclei blue (acidic/basophilic structures); eosin stains cytoplasm pink/red (basic/eosinophilic structures).

title: Name four special stains and what each detects.
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Name four special stains and what each detects.
body.back: PAS: glycogen and mucin. Perls: iron/haemosiderin. Von Kossa: calcification. Congo red: amyloid (apple-green birefringence under polarised light). Masson's trichrome: fibrosis/collagen.

title: What is a frozen section and what is its main drawback?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is a frozen section and what is its main drawback?
body.back: A rapid intraoperative technique: the sample is frozen and cut on a cryostat for same-day diagnosis (margins, metastases, unknown lesions). Drawback: lower section quality than paraffin, so it must be confirmed on permanent sections.

title: What is immunohistochemistry (IHC)?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is immunohistochemistry (IHC)?
body.back: Detection of a specific antigen using an antibody linked to an enzyme or fluorochrome, producing a visible coloured reaction under the microscope.

title: Forensic vs clinical/academic autopsy?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Forensic vs clinical/academic autopsy?
body.back: Forensic: performed when death may be a criminal matter. Clinical/academic: performed to determine an uncertain medical cause of death, audit diagnoses, teach, or for research.

title: How long is 10% formalin fixation typically needed, and in what volume?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: How long is 10% formalin fixation typically needed, and in what volume?
body.back: 1 to a few hours for biopsies, 24–72 hours for surgical specimens; the fixative volume should be at least 10–15 times the tissue bulk.

title: How long are paraffin blocks and slides archived?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: How long are paraffin blocks and slides archived?
body.back: At least 10 years, and lifelong for paediatric pathology, allowing second opinions and further IHC or molecular studies.

title: What must always follow a positive or uncertain cytology result before aggressive treatment?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What must always follow a positive or uncertain cytology result before aggressive treatment?
body.back: Histological confirmation via biopsy — cytology alone is a screening/guidance test, not a final diagnosis.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Section cutting. Microtome sections of 3 to 5 microns floated on a warm water bath.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Fixation. 10% formalin, 1 to a few hours for biopsies, 24 to 72 h for specimens, volume 10 to 15 times the tissue.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Frozen section. Cryostat during surgery; rapid but lower quality, confirmed on paraffin.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Grossing. Physician plus technician: measure, orient, ink margins, select sections into engraved cassettes.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Microscopy and ancillary tests. Pathologist reads several levels; may add IHC or molecular biology.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Processing and embedding. Graded alcohols, clearing, paraffin impregnation, then a paraffin block.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Report and archiving. Signed report; blocks and slides kept at least 10 years.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Sample and request form. Fresh sample transported within 30 minutes with a completed request form.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Staining. H&E standard: haematoxylin blue nuclei, eosin pink cytoplasm; special stains on demand.

title: List the sources of samples sent to pathology.
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: List the sources of samples sent to pathology.
body.back: Operating room, endoscopy, radiology (guided biopsies), hospital wards, private practices.

title: Rules for a good biopsy?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Rules for a good biopsy?
body.back: Numerous and large enough; centred on the lesion (sometimes with healthy tissue); oriented when needed; good quality without crush or electrocoagulation artefact; labelled if multiple.

title: What information must a request form contain?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What information must a request form contain?
body.back: Patient identification, requesting physician, procedure date, clinical history and examination, biological and radiological work-up, organ and orientation, intraoperative findings, prior surgery/diagnosis/treatment, whether rapid diagnosis is needed.

title: What happens at grossing?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What happens at grossing?
body.back: Physician and technician count and measure biopsies into cassettes; orient, measure, weigh and document specimens; ink the margins; select sections for microscopy.

title: Why is tissue processing critical?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Why is tissue processing critical?
body.back: It takes long and mistakes force repetition; under- or over-processing destroys detail; the tissue must be neither too soft nor too hard for sectioning.

title: Describe paraffin embedding.
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Describe paraffin embedding.
body.back: Impregnated tissue is placed in a mould of molten wax, oriented with the cutting surface at the base, topped with the labelled cassette, cooled at -15°C to form a firm block.

title: Uses of an autopsy?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Uses of an autopsy?
body.back: Determine cause of death; audit clinical diagnoses; education; research; statistics.

title: Applications of cytopathology?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Applications of cytopathology?
body.back: Screening of asymptomatic cancer (cervical), diagnosis of symptomatic cancer, follow-up of treated patients; minimally invasive, cheap, rapid.

title: When is frozen section NOT indicated?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: When is frozen section NOT indicated?
body.back: When the result has no immediate implication for surgical decisions, or when the tissue is unique/small and needed for permanent processing.

title: Why is the pathological report so important?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Why is the pathological report so important?
body.back: Signed, under the pathologist's responsibility, standardised to international norms and often illustrated — it is the key element for treatment decisions.

title: Three layers of a blood vessel and their contents?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Three layers of a blood vessel and their contents?
body.back: Intima: endothelium (internal elastic lamina below). Media: smooth muscle (external elastic lamina). Adventitia: connective tissue with nerves and vasa vasorum.

title: Starling forces: what pushes fluid out and what pulls it in?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Starling forces: what pushes fluid out and what pulls it in?
body.back: Capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out (higher at the arteriolar end); plasma oncotic pressure (albumin) pulls it in (dominant at the venular end); interstitial pressures oppose; lymphatics drain the residual excess.

title: Transudate vs exudate?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Transudate vs exudate?
body.back: Transudate: protein <3 g/dL, few cells, clear, SG <1.016, non-inflammatory (heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic). Exudate: protein >3 g/dL, many cells, cloudy, SG >1.020, inflammatory (infection, cancer).

title: Five major mechanisms of oedema with an example each.
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Five major mechanisms of oedema with an example each.
body.back: ↑Hydrostatic pressure (heart failure, DVT); ↓oncotic pressure (nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis); ↑permeability (inflammation, burns); lymphatic obstruction (mastectomy, filariasis); Na/water retention (renal failure, hyperaldosteronism).

title: How is oedema classified?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: How is oedema classified?
body.back: By distribution: localised vs generalised (anasarca). By composition: transudative vs exudative. By physical character: pitting (cardiac/renal/hepatic) vs non-pitting (lymphoedema, lipoedema, myxoedema).

title: Inflammatory vs haemodynamic oedema?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Inflammatory vs haemodynamic oedema?
body.back: Inflammatory: ↑permeability via histamine, bradykinin, TNF-α, IL-1 → protein-rich exudate with neutrophils and fibrin. Haemodynamic: altered Starling forces → protein-poor transudate (cardiogenic, renal, hepatic).

title: Causes and signs of pulmonary oedema?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Causes and signs of pulmonary oedema?
body.back: Left heart failure, ARDS, toxin inhalation, severe infection, high altitude (HAPE). Dyspnoea, wheeze, pink frothy sputum; may coexist with pleural effusion.

title: Causes and signs of cerebral oedema?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Causes and signs of cerebral oedema?
body.back: Trauma, stroke, meningitis/encephalitis, tumour, hyponatraemia, toxins. Headache, confusion, seizures, coma; macroscopically narrow sulci and flat gyri.

title: Define lymphoedema and give causes.
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Define lymphoedema and give causes.
body.back: Non-pitting swelling from lymphatic damage or blockage: surgery (radical mastectomy), radiation, cancer, filariasis (elephantiasis), or congenital. Persistent heaviness and skin thickening.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Arteriolar end. Hydrostatic pressure from the heart pushes fluid out.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Capillary. Endothelium without media; the site of exchange.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Increased hydrostatic pressure. Heart failure, DVT, venous obstruction.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Lymphatic obstruction. Lymphoedema after mastectomy, filariasis, tumour.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Lymphatic drainage. Removes the small residual excess of interstitial fluid.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Reduced oncotic pressure. Nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis, malnutrition.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Increased permeability. Inflammation, burns: protein-rich exudate.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Sodium and water retention. Renal failure, hyperaldosteronism via renin, aldosterone and ADH.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Venular end. Plasma oncotic pressure from albumin pulls fluid back.

title: Arteries by type?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Arteries by type?
body.back: Large elastic (aorta, elastin-rich media), medium muscular (coronary, renal, smooth-muscle media), small arteries and arterioles within organs.

title: Regulation of haemodynamics?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Regulation of haemodynamics?
body.back: Neural (baroreceptors, chemoreceptors, sympathetic/parasympathetic), hormonal (RAAS, ADH), local (autoregulation, nitric oxide, endothelin).

title: Consequences of vascular wall changes?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Consequences of vascular wall changes?
body.back: Narrowing: slow (atherosclerosis → atrophy/infarction) or acute (thrombus/embolus → infarction). Weakening: dilatation, dissection, rupture.

title: Body water distribution?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Body water distribution?
body.back: 60% of body weight is water; two-thirds intracellular, one-third extracellular (intravascular, interstitial, transcellular).

title: Normal fluid circulation in one sentence?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Normal fluid circulation in one sentence?
body.back: Hydrostatic pressure at the arteriolar end pushes fluid out, oncotic pressure at the venular end pulls it back, and lymphatics drain the small residue.

title: Mechanism of oedema by sodium retention?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Mechanism of oedema by sodium retention?
body.back: Hypovolaemia → renal vasoconstriction, ↓GFR, ↑renin/aldosterone and ↑ADH → retention of Na and water → oedema.

title: Localised vs generalised oedema?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Localised vs generalised oedema?
body.back: Localised: trauma, infection/cellulitis, insect bites, DVT — swelling, redness, pain, warmth. Generalised (anasarca): heart, kidney, liver failure, protein deficiency.

title: What is pitting oedema and its causes?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: What is pitting oedema and its causes?
body.back: Indentation persists after pressure; from water retention in heart, kidney, liver disease, DVT, varicose veins, thrombophlebitis, pregnancy.

title: Types of haemodynamic oedema?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Types of haemodynamic oedema?
body.back: Cardiogenic (venous congestion), renal (nephrotic hypoalbuminaemia, sodium retention), hepatic (cirrhosis).

title: Peripheral oedema causes?
subject: subj:pathanat

body.front: Peripheral oedema causes?
body.back: Venous insufficiency, congestive heart failure, kidney disease, lymphatic obstruction; also age, pregnancy, hypertension.
